subject: physics
title: Waves
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Waves.

concepts.def: A wave that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy travel, like light; only these can be polarised.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.
When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
Formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along itself.
The difference in distance from two coherent sources to a point; whole-wavelength differences give constructive interference.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Waves — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Waves brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Waves.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which type of wave can be polarised?
options: Longitudinal waves only
Both transverse and longitudinal waves
Neither type of wave
Transverse waves only

mcqs.q: At a node on a stationary wave:
options: The displacement is always zero.
The amplitude is at its maximum.
The wave moves fastest.
The wavelength is zero.

mcqs.q: Two coherent sources interfere constructively at a point when the path difference is:
options: A whole number of wavelengths
An odd number of half wavelengths
Any value at all
Always exactly half a wavelength

mcqs.q: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. Using v = fλ, its speed is:
options: 54 m/s

mcqs.q: Do all points on a stationary wave oscillate with the same amplitude?
options: No — amplitude varies from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinodes.
Yes — but only underwater.
Yes — amplitude is constant along the wave, as in a progressive wave.
No — amplitude is largest at the nodes.

mcqs.q: When a wave refracts into a new medium, which property stays the same?
options: The frequency — the speed and wavelength change together.
Everything about the wave changes.
The wavelength stays the same and the frequency changes.
Yes — but only underwater.
No — amplitude is largest at the nodes.
Yes — but only underwater.
No — polarisation applies only to transverse waves, and sound is longitudinal.
Yes — any wave can be polarised with the right filter.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Transverse wave”?
options: A wave that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.
A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy travel, like light; only these can be polarised.
The difference in distance from two coherent sources to a point; whole-wavelength differences give constructive interference.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Stationary wave”?
options: A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.
When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy travel, like light; only these can be polarised.
Formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along itself.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Longitudinal wave”?
options: The difference in distance from two coherent sources to a point; whole-wavelength differences give constructive interference.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.
Formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along itself.
When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Progressive wave”?
options: When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
A wave that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
Formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along itself.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Superposition”?
options: The difference in distance from two coherent sources to a point; whole-wavelength differences give constructive interference.
When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
A wave that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy travel, like light; only these can be polarised.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Path difference”?
options: Formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along itself.
When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy travel, like sound.
The difference in distance from two coherent sources to a point; whole-wavelength differences give constructive interference.
